name: 5-Amino-1MQ
lead: 5-Amino-1MQ (5-amino-1-methylquinolinium) is a small-molecule inhibitor of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT), an enzyme involved in cellular NAD+ and methyl-group metabolism. It carries a permanent positive charge and is therefore handled as a salt, usually the chloride or iodide. Wikipedia notes that it has been sold as a gray-market weight-loss product, sometimes described as a peptide, although it is an experimental small molecule and not a peptide.[1]

Research on it consists of cell and mouse experiments. In a 2018 mouse study, membrane-permeable NNMT inhibitors of this chemical family reversed diet-induced obesity.[3] Wikipedia states that no formal toxicity studies or human clinical trial results exist.[1] The compound is not an approved medicine.
In online communities it is discussed as an oral or injectable fat-loss and metabolism product, an extrapolation from the rodent findings rather than from human data.
infobox: Not approved for medical use; sold as research chemical or supplement [1][2]

paras: 5-Amino-1MQ is a quaternary ammonium compound built on a bicyclic quinolinium core with a methyl group on the ring nitrogen and an amino group at position 5.[2] Because the nitrogen is permanently charged, it is supplied as a salt such as the iodide.[1][2] It is not a peptide, a point Wikipedia emphasises because it is sometimes marketed alongside peptides.[1]

Grokipedia, which is AI-generated and may contain errors, describes the iodide salt as a colored powder soluble in polar solvents and reports a half-maximal inhibitory concentration against NNMT of about 1.2 micromolar from the original characterisation work.[2]

NNMT transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to nicotinamide, producing 1-methylnicotinamide. Its expression is higher in fat tissue in obesity and type 2 diabetes in several reports, which prompted interest in it as a drug target.[4] Inhibiting the enzyme in cultured fat cells is reported to lower 1-methylnicotinamide and raise intracellular NAD+ and related metabolic markers.[2][3]
Researchers hypothesise that this shifts adipocyte metabolism toward energy expenditure and reduces lipid accumulation, although the downstream mechanisms are still under investigation.[3][4]
Human pharmacokinetic data have not been published. Mouse studies used injections of the compound, and published descriptions of the membrane-permeable inhibitors concern rodent tissue exposure.[3]
No studies found in humans. Wikipedia states that the compound has no human clinical trial results and no formal toxicity studies.[1]

Related research (animal): In mice fed a high-fat diet, selective membrane-permeable NNMT inhibitors reduced body weight and white adipose mass, reduced adipocyte size and improved metabolic markers without a change in food intake, according to the 2018 study.[3] A 2021 Scientific Reports study in mice combined NNMT inhibition with a reduced-calorie diet and described a distinct progression of metabolic responses.[5] A review of NNMT in obesity and type 2 diabetes summarises the preclinical and observational literature on the enzyme as a target.[4]

Human safety, interactions and long-term effects are unknown. Because NNMT consumes methyl donors and affects NAD+ metabolism, the consequences of chronic inhibition in people have not been evaluated in published work.[4] The compound is not approved by any regulator and is sold as a research chemical or supplement of unverified purity.[1][2]

The compound is marketed to people seeking fat loss and described as a way to raise NAD+ and metabolic rate. Community use follows supplier and influencer descriptions of the mouse results, and no controlled human outcome data are available to compare with these accounts.[1][2]

timeline.event: Mouse study reports membrane-permeable NNMT inhibitors reverse high-fat-diet obesity.[3]
Review of NNMT in obesity and type 2 diabetes published.[4]
Mouse study combines NNMT inhibition with calorie restriction.[5]

lore.intro: The compound circulates in fat-loss supplement and peptide-adjacent marketing as an NAD+ and metabolism booster, with claims derived from mouse data.[1][2]

claims.claim: 5-Amino-1MQ burns fat by inhibiting NNMT and raising NAD+
claims.believers: Sellers and users cite the mouse studies in which NNMT inhibition reduced fat mass without a change in food intake.[2][3]
claims.experts: The studies were in mice and cell culture; Wikipedia notes there are no human trial results.[1][3]

claims.claim: It is a peptide like other injectable research compounds
claims.believers: Some gray-market sellers list it alongside peptides.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states it is a quinolinium small molecule and not a peptide.[1]

claims.believers: Mouse studies reported no change in food intake and no obvious toxicity at tested doses, as summarised by Grokipedia.[2]
claims.experts: No formal toxicity studies or human safety data exist.[1]
